research:
**Rundown: Senegal National Assembly dissolution before January 1, 2027**

**Current state (as of Nov 24, 2026)**
- The Assembly has 165 seats. PASTEF holds 130 of them, and Ousmane Sonko has presided over the Assembly since May 2026.
- The split began when President Faye dismissed Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko and dissolved his cabinet on May 22. Sonko was elected president of the Assembly on 26 May with 132 of the 133 votes cast, in a vote boycotted by the opposition.
- Budget standoff: Deputies rejected the revised finance law on November 3 by 109 votes to 20. Faye then put the revised 2026 budget into force by decree, bypassing the Assembly. The decree was signed November 19 and announced around November 20–21. The Assembly had also thrown out the first part of the 2027 budget a day earlier.
- On November 17, PASTEF struck Faye and 31 others off its membership rolls.
- Dissolution talk: Multiple outlets say the power opens in early December. One says from December 2 the president will hold the constitutional power to dissolve the Assembly, an option now openly discussed in Dakar. Earlier, in July, President Faye referred to the Constitutional Council the possibility of pairing legislative and local elections. Opposition figure Talla Sylla has publicly urged dissolution in December 2026.
- I found no official announcement or decree of dissolution as of today.

**Legal constraint and timing**
- Article 87 is the dissolution clause. The president may dissolve the Assembly by decree after hearing the prime minister and the Assembly's president, but dissolution cannot happen during the first two years of a legislature.
- The current legislature opened on December 2, 2024, so the bar lifts on about December 2, 2026. The Presidency's spokesman has said dissolution stays barred until around that date. Sources differ slightly on the exact day: Carnegie says "until at least December 2026," and Brookings says "November 2026." The most specific sources point to December 2.
- The Constitution also bars dissolution while emergency powers are in use, under Article 52. The Presidency spokesman argues Article 52 does not block dissolution. I did not verify whether any emergency powers are currently in force, so this is an open point.
- Election timing: a dissolution decree must set the election between 60 and 90 days after its publication. A decree in December would therefore put elections roughly in February–March 2027. Deputies keep their mandates until the new Assembly's election is proclaimed.
- The 2-year bar ends December 2, which leaves about four weeks (December 2–31) in the window. Any dissolution before year-end would need to happen in that span.

**Scheduled events before the window closes**
- I did not find a confirmed date for the dissolution decision or for the local elections. One source says local elections are "looming," but I found no date.
- I did not find the 2027 budget timetable. This matters because a budget deadlock is the main stated driver of dissolution talk.

**Base rates**
- Faye dissolved the Assembly once before, on September 12, 2024, calling snap elections for November 17, 2024. That dissolution came after the required waiting period and was tied to a push for a stronger mandate. A move that pairs dissolution with local elections would be rare, if not unprecedented, in Senegal.
- Commentators also note the political costs. One analysis argues that an election that follows dissolution would pit Faye against Sonko in a proxy battle.

**Resolution if nothing changes**
- If no dissolution decree is issued by December 31, 2026, the question resolves No. Faye is legally barred until about December 2, and nothing I found shows a decision has been made.
- A Yes would need a formal decree (signed and published, or otherwise formally issued) between about December 2 and December 31. Credible sources would need to report it. Some ambiguity could arise if a decree is signed in late December but published in January.

---
## Second research pass (base rate, primary source, the case against)
**Base rate.** Since the 2001 constitution, I found two dissolutions. Wade dissolved the assembly after the new constitution was approved, before the April 2001 election (President Wade dissolved the assembly and, following new elections, his coalition controlled 89 of 120 seats.). Faye's dissolution came on 12 September 2024. That is two in about 25 years, or under 1% per month on this record. I did not verify the Sall-era record, and the current crisis makes the conditional rate much higher than the unconditional one.

**Primary source.** I did not reach the Journal officiel or the Presidency site, so I have no first-hand decree check. The latest decree I found is No. 2026-2416 of 19 November, which put the revised budget into force. Pastef's resolution against it was filed on 20 November and was examined on Tuesday 24 November by the Finance and Laws committees. Faye's latest dissolution statement dates from 24 September, when he said there is no date set for dissolving the National Assembly or for holding elections on any particular date.

**Already decided?** Nothing I found indicates this. The legal bar runs until 2 December, and the Presidency's stance is that nothing has been fixed. No dissolution decree has been reported.

**Strongest evidence against a Yes:**
- Faye's September statement above, which is the last official word I found.
- Minister Boubacar Camara said 2 December is not binding on Diomaye Faye, and that the president is not obliged to dissolve.
- One legal analysis argues Faye must first set the local election date before signing a dissolution decree (a legal analysis considers he must first set the date of the local elections before signing a dissolution decree). This is a single commentator, and I could not confirm it against the text.
- The timing is tight. Article 87 requires voting 60 to 90 days after publication (the ballot takes place at least sixty days and at most ninety days after publication). A decree signed in December therefore points to a vote in early 2027, and only about four weeks of the window remain.
- Article 52 bars dissolution while exceptional powers are in use (The National Assembly may not be dissolved during the exercise of the exceptional powers.). I did not check whether any such powers are in force.

**Not found:** any decree, any local election date, the 2027 budget timetable, and the Sall-era dissolution record.
title: Will Senegal's National Assembly be dissolved before January 1, 2027?
